title: Bodies, Hubs, and Disembodied Minds: Grounded Sensorimotor Simulation vs. Amodal Symbolic Representation — Harnad's symbol grounding problem vs Fodorian Mentalese; Barsalou's multimodal simulations & van Dantzig's physical-to-conceptual modality-switch cost; Patterson's semantic dementia anterior temporal hub-and-spoke synthesis & Boulenger-Pulvermüller's motor idiom fMRI; Mahon & Caramazza's apraxia spreading-activation critique, Bedny's congenitally blind occipital language plasticity, Wagenmakers' N=1,894 pen-in-mouth collapse (+0.82 to +0.03) & disembodied LLMs; 159 ms ATL-to-M1 cascade math & congenital limb-absence RSA TOST protocols

teenKit.tldr: When you read words like 'cinnamon' or 'kick', does your brain simulate the physical experience, or does it process abstract algebraic symbols like a computer? Cognitive science has been locked in a massive 35-year war over how meaning is actually built inside your head.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how your brain turns ink on a page into vivid sensory realities shapes everything from how we treat brain injuries and semantic dementia to how we build artificial intelligence that actually understands what it says.
keyTakeaways: Grounded cognition claims that understanding words like 'hammer' requires your brain to literally reenact sensory and motor experiences in your visual and motor cortices.
The hub-and-spoke model bridges the debate by showing how sensory details are managed by local brain regions while the anterior temporal lobe acts as a central switchboard to pull it all together.

Strong embodiment theories have taken major hits from replication crises (like the pen-in-mouth facial feedback collapse) and evidence from congenitally blind adults who process grammar using visual brain areas.

vocab.meaning: The theory that your brain understands concepts by physically reenacting sensory and motor experiences related to them.
The old-school computer-like theory that words are stored as abstract, disembodied algebraic tokens stripped of sensory detail.
The central hub in your brain that acts like a master switchboard to synthesize scattered sensory details into a unified concept.
The tiny delay your brain experiences when it has to rapidly jump from processing one type of sensory information to another.

quiz.question: What is the core claim of grounded and embodied cognition?
options: The brain stores all language as pure algebraic formulas.
Understanding a word requires your brain to simulate the physical and sensory experiences tied to it.
Language is entirely processed by the cerebellum without involving the cortex.
Words have no physical basis in human biology.
quiz.explanation: Grounded cognition argues that thinking about actions or objects literally triggers your brain's sensory and motor networks.

quiz.question: What role does the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) play in semantic memory according to the hub-and-spoke model?
options: It acts as a central transmodal hub that synthesizes distributed sensory spokes into a coherent concept.
It exclusively processes auditory tones and spoken language.
It stores abstract math symbols while ignoring physical sensations.
It acts as a permanent storage locker that never communicates with the motor cortex.
quiz.explanation: The ATL functions as the central hub tying together scattered sensory features from different brain regions.

quiz.question: What major blow did Eric-Jan Wagenmakers's 1,894-person replication deal to strong embodiment theories?
options: It proved that blind people cannot process spatial language.
It showed that the anterior temporal lobe is completely optional for human speech.
It collapsed Fritz Strack's classic pen-in-mouth facial feedback effect from a massive 0.82 down to a near-zero 0.03.
It proved that AI models have richer emotional lives than humans.
quiz.explanation: The massive registered replication report drastically shrank the classic facial feedback effect, challenging strict bodily simulation claims.
